t: Closest Divisors — Factor Search Around the Square Root
o: We must pick either num+1 or num+2, factor it into two factors a*b = n, and return the pair with the smallest |a-b|. The closest pair for any n is found by taking the largest divisor a of n with a <= sqrt(n); then b = n/a and the gap b-a is minimized. Since num <= 10^9, n <= 10^9+2, so trial division up to sqrt(n) (~31623 iterations) is trivially fast. For example, num=8: 9=3*3 (gap 0) beats 10=2*5 (gap 3), so answer is [3,3]. For num=123: 124=4*31 (gap 27) vs 125=5*25 (gap 20), so [5,25].
k: The closest factor pair of n is always (largest divisor <= sqrt(n), n divided by it).
Only two candidates exist: num+1 and num+2; evaluate both and keep the pair with smaller difference.
Trial division up to sqrt(n) suffices since n <= ~1e9, giving O(sqrt(num)) time.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute force from sqrt(n) downward
a.i: For each candidate n in {num+1, num+2}, scan i from floor(sqrt(n)) down to 1; the first i dividing n gives the most balanced pair (i, n/i), because as i decreases the gap strictly grows. Compare the best pairs from both candidates by their difference.
s: Define helper best(n): loop i from int(sqrt(n)) down to 1; return [i, n//i] at first divisor.
Compute p1 = best(num+1) and p2 = best(num+2).
Return whichever pair has smaller second-minus-first difference.
a.t: O(sqrt(num)) — two trial-division loops each run at most sqrt(1e9+2) ≈ 31623 iterations.
a.sp: O(1) — only a few variables besides the output.

a.i: Equivalent to Approach 1 but iterate upward from ceil(sqrt(n)) checking whether n % i == 0; if yes, the pair is (n/i, i). This avoids relying on floating-point sqrt precision issues in edge cases and terminates quickly because some divisor is always found at or above sqrt(n) (namely n itself).
s: For candidate n, start i = floor(sqrt(n)) + 1.
Return [n // i, i]; compare candidates num+1 and num+2 by gap.
a.t: O(sqrt(num)) — same bound; worst case when n is prime we walk from sqrt(n)+1 up to n, but that still fits easily within limits... actually bounded by O(n) only for primes near 1e9, which is why Approach 1's downward scan is preferred in practice.

w: In an interview, present Approach 1: it has a guaranteed tight O(sqrt(num)) bound regardless of primality, whereas the upward scan can degrade toward O(n) when a candidate is prime. Key pitfalls: integer overflow when computing num+2 in fixed-width languages (use 64-bit), floating-point sqrt inaccuracies near perfect squares (prefer integer sqrt like Python's math.isqrt or adjust with a correction step), and forgetting to compare gaps between the two candidates rather than just returning one. Edge cases: num=1 gives 2=[1,2] vs 3=[1,3], answer [1,2]; num such that num+1 is a perfect square yields a zero-gap pair immediately. Follow-ups might ask about factoring much larger numbers (would need Pollard's rho) or returning all factor pairs.
